blocks.html:
Exposé II
TOPOLOGIES AND SHEAVESby J.L. Verdier

After the definition of topologies and pretopologies (n° 1) and of sheaves of sets (n° 2), we take up in n° 3 the central theorem of this exposé (3.4): the existence of the sheaf associated to a presheaf. In order to cover all the cases encountered in practice, the existence of this functor is proved for presheaves on a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (3.0.2). Sections n° 4 and n° 5 draw the consequences of this theorem on the behaviour of inductive and projective limits in categories of sheaves. In n° 6 we define and study sheaves with values in arbitrary categories, in order to focus attention at once on sheaves of rings, of groups, of modules, etc.
1. Topologies, covering families, pretopologies

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

A topology on a category \(C\) is the datum, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), of a set \(J(X)\) of sieves of \(X\), this datum being subject to the following axioms:

  1. (T 1)

    (Stability under base change). For every object \(X\) of \(C\), every sieve \(R \in J(X)\), every morphism \(f : Y \to X\) (\(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\,(C)\)), the sieve \(R \times_X Y\) of \(Y\) belongs to \(J(Y)\).

  2. (T 2)

    (Local character). If \(R\) and \(R'\) are two sieves of \(X\), if \(R \in J(X)\), and if for every \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\,(C)\) and every morphism \(Y \to R\) the sieve \(R' \times_X Y\) belongs to \(J(Y)\), then \(R'\) belongs to \(J(X)\).

  3. (T 3)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\), \(X\) belongs to \(J(X)\).

The sieves belonging to \(J(X)\) will be called the sieves covering \(X\), or also the refinements of \(X\). From the axioms (T1), (T2), (T3), one deduces immediately that the set of sieves covering \(X\) is stable under finite intersections, and that every sieve containing a covering sieve is a covering sieve. The set \(J(X)\), ordered by inclusion, is therefore cofiltered (I 8).

Let \(C\) be a category, and \(T\) and \(T'\) two topologies on \(C\). The topology \(T\) is said to be finer than the topology \(T'\) if for every object \(X\) of \(C\), every refinement of \(X\) for the topology \(T'\) is a refinement of \(X\) for the topology \(T\). In this way one defines an order structure on the set of topologies.

Let \((T_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of topologies on \(C\). The sets, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), of the sieves of \(X\) that are covering for all the topologies \(T_i\), satisfy the axioms (T 1), (T 2) and (T 3) and therefore define a topology: the intersection topology of the \(T_i\), i.e. the infimum of the \(T_i\). It is the finest of the topologies that is less fine than all the topologies \(T_i\). The family \((T_i)_{i \in I}\) consequently admits a supremum: the intersection topology of the topologies finer than each of the \(T_i\).
In particular the datum \(J(X) = \) the set of all the sieves of \(X\) is a topology finer than every topology on \(C\), which we shall call the discrete topology.
There exists a topology less fine than every topology on \(C\); the topology for which \(J(X) = \{X\}\) for every \(X\) of \(C\). This topology is called the coarse topology or chaotic topology.
A category \(C\) equipped with a topology is called a site. The category \(C\) is called the category underlying the site.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.2

Let \(C\) be a site, and \(X\) an object of \(C\). A family of morphisms \((f_\alpha : X_\alpha \to X)\), \(\alpha \in A\), is said to be covering if the sieve generated by the family \(f_\alpha\) (I 4.3.3) is a sieve covering \(X\).

Let \(C\) be a category. For each object \(X\) of \(C\), let us give ourselves a set of families of morphisms with target \(X\). There then exists a topology \(T\) which is the least fine of the topologies for which the given families are covering, namely the intersection (1.1.3) of all the topologies in question. This topology is called the topology generated by the given sets of families of morphisms. It is difficult to describe, in general, all the covering sieves of this topology. However the situation is more pleasant in the following case:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.3

Let \(C\) be a category. A pretopology on \(C\) is the datum, for each object \(X\) of \(C\), of a set \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) of families of morphisms with target \(X\), this datum being subject to the following axioms:

  1. (PT 0)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\), the morphisms of the families of morphisms of \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) are squarable. (Recall that a morphism \(Y \to X\) is said to be squarable if for every morphism \(Z \to X\) the fibre product \(Z \times_X Y\) is representable).

  2. (PT 1)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\), every family \((X_\alpha \to X)_{\alpha \in A}\) belonging to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\), and every morphism \(Y \to X\) (\(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\,(C)\)), the family: \((X_\alpha \times_X Y \to Y)_{\alpha \in A}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\). (Stability under base change).

  3. (PT 2)

    If \((X_\alpha \to X)_{\alpha \in A}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) and if for each \(\alpha \in A\), \((X_{\beta_\alpha} \to X_\alpha)_{\beta_\alpha \in B_\alpha}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X_\alpha)\), then the family \((X_\gamma \to X)_{\gamma \in \coprod_{\alpha \in A} B_\alpha}\) (where for every \(\gamma = (\alpha, \beta_\alpha)\), \(\alpha \in A\), \(\beta_\alpha \in B_\alpha\), the morphism \(X_\gamma \to X\) is the composite morphism: \(X_\gamma = X_{\beta_\alpha} \to X_\alpha \to X\)) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\). (Stability under composition).

  4. (PT 3)

    The family: \(X \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{id}_X\ } X\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\).

The definition of 1.1.6 allows us to consider, for a given pretopology on \(C\), the topology on \(C\) generated by this pretopology. Note that if \(C\) is a category in which the fibre products are representable, then every topology \(T\) of \(C\) can be defined by a pretopology, namely the one for which \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) is formed of all the families covering \(X\) for the topology \(T\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4

Let \(C\) be a category, \(E\) a pretopology on \(C\), \(T\) the topology defined by the pretopology \(E\) (1.1.6), and \(X\) an object of \(C\). Denote by \(J_E(X)\) the set of sieves of \(X\) generated by the families of the pretopology, and by \(J_T(X)\) the set of refinements of \(X\) for the topology \(T\). Then \(J_E(X)\) is cofinal in \(J_T(X)\). In other words, for a sieve \(R\) of \(X\) to belong to \(J_T(X)\), it is necessary and sufficient that there exist a sieve \(R' \in J_E(X)\) such that \(R' \subset R\).

Proof. For every object \(X\) of \(C\), let \(J'(X)\) be the set of sieves of \(X\) that contain a sieve of \(J_E(X)\). One evidently has \(J'(X) \subset J_T(X)\). To show that \(J'(X) = J_T(X)\), it suffices to show that the data of the \(J'(X)\) define a topology on \(C\). Now the \(J'(X)\) evidently satisfy the axioms (T 1) and (T 3). It therefore remains to verify (T 2). For this it suffices to prove that if \(R'\) is a subsieve of \(R \in J_E(X)\) such that for every \(Y \to R\), the sieve \(R' \times_X Y\) of \(Y\) belongs to \(J'(X)\), then the sieve \(R'\) belongs to \(J'(X)\). Now the sieve \(R\) is generated by a family \((X_\alpha \to X)\) belonging to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\), and for every \(\alpha\) the sieve \(R' \times_X X_\alpha\) contains a sieve generated by a family \((X_{\beta_\alpha} \to X_\alpha)\) belonging to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X_\alpha)\). One deduces that the sieve \(R'\) contains a sieve generated by the family \((X_{\beta_\alpha} \to X)\). Therefore, by axiom (PT 2), \(R'\) contains a sieve of \(J_E(X)\) and consequently belongs to \(J'(X)\), q.e.d.
2. Sheaves of sets

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1

Let \(C\) be a site whose underlying category is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. A presheaf \(F\) with values in \(\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) is said to be separated (resp. is a sheaf) if for every sieve \(R\) covering \(X\), an object of \(C\), the map: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F) \] is an injection (resp. a bijection). The full subcategory of \(\widehat{C}\) whose objects are the sheaves is called the category of sheaves of sets on \(C\), and is most often denoted \(\widetilde{C}\) (1). When no ambiguity results from it, we shall say simply category of sheaves on \(C\); on the other hand we shall sometimes be more precise by saying category of sheaves with values in \(\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\), or again category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and \(\mathscr{F} = (F_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves on \(C\). For each object \(X\) of \(C\), denote by \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\) the set of sieves \(R \hookrightarrow X\) of \(C\) such that for every morphism \(Y \to X\) of \(C\) with target \(X\), the sieve \(R \times_X Y\) has the following property: the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,F_i) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R \times_X Y, F_i) \] is bijective (resp. injective) for every \(i \in I\). Then the sets \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\) define a topology on \(C\), which is the finest of the topologies for which each of the \(F_i\) is a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf).
Proof. The \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\) evidently satisfy the axioms (T 1) and (T 3). It remains to show that they satisfy (T 2). For this it suffices to show that:

1) If \(R' \hookrightarrow R \hookrightarrow X\) are two sieves of \(X\), such that \(R \in J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\) and such that for every \(Y \to R\) (where \(Y\) is an object of \(C\)) the sieve \(R' \times_X Y\) belongs to \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(Y)\), then the sieve \(R'\) belongs to \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\).
2) If \(R' \hookrightarrow R \hookrightarrow X\) are two sieves of \(X\) such that \(R' \in J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\), then the sieve \(R\) belongs to \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\).

Note that, in case 2), for every \(Y \to R\) (where \(Y\) is an object of \(C\)) the sieve \(R' \times_X Y\) belongs to \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(Y)\). Now, in cases 1) and 2), \(R\) is the inductive limit of the \(Y\), objects of \(C\), over \(R\) (I 3.4). The inductive limits in \(\widehat{C}\) are universal (I 3.3). Consequently in cases 1) and 2), \(R'\) is the inductive limit of the \(R' \times_X Y\). Now, in cases 1) and (2), \(R' \times_X Y\) belongs to \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(Y)\). One deduces, by passing to the inductive limit over the objects \(Y\) of \(C\) over \(R\), that the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F_i) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R',F_i) \] is a bijection (resp. an injection) for every \(i \in I\). Consequently the maps \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,F_i) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R',F_i) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,F_i) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F_i) \] are, in cases 1) and 2), bijections (resp. injections). Moreover, the hypotheses 1) and 2) are visibly stable under arbitrary base change \(Y \to X\) (\(Y\) an object of \(C\)). One then deduces that for every object \(Y\) of \(C\) over \(X\) and every \(i \in I\), the maps \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,F_i) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R \times_X Y, F_i) \] \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,F_i) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R' \times_X Y, F_i) \] are in both cases bijections (resp. injections); which shows that \(R'\) and \(R\) belong to \(J_{\mathscr{F}}(X)\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and for every \(X\) of \(C\) a set \(K(X)\) of sieves of \(X\). Suppose that the \(K(X)\) satisfy axiom (T 1) of (1.1). For a presheaf \(F\) to be a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf) for the topology generated (1.1.6) by the \(K(X)\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every sieve \(R \in K(X)\), the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F) \] be a bijection (resp. an injection).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

In particular, let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category equipped with a pretopology. For a presheaf \(F\) to be a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf), it is necessary and sufficient that for every object \(X\) of \(C\) and for every family \((X_\alpha \to X)\) belonging to \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\), the diagram of sets \[ F(X) \longrightarrow \prod_{\alpha \in A} F(X_\alpha) \rightrightarrows \prod_{(\alpha,\beta) \in A \times A} F(X_\alpha \times_X X_\beta) \] be exact (resp. the map \[ F(X) \longrightarrow \prod_{\alpha \in A} F(X_\alpha) \] be injective).
Proof. One applies 2.3, then (I 3.5) and (I 2.12).
With corollary 2.4 one recovers the definition given in [1].

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.5

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. The canonical topology of \(C\) is the finest topology for which the representable functors are sheaves (2.2). A sieve covering \(X\) for the canonical topology will be called a universal strict epimorphic sieve. A covering family for the canonical topology will be called a universal strict epimorphic family. When moreover the morphisms of the covering family are squarable, the family will be said to be universal effective epimorphic [2].

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.5.1

For almost all the sites that one has had to use up to now, the topology is less fine than the canonical topology; in other words, the representable functors on \(C\) are sheaves, i.e. the covering families of \(C\) are universal strict epimorphic. The only exception to this rule is the site \(\widehat{C}\) studied in n° 5 (whose topology is finer, and most often strictly finer, than the canonical topology).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6

For a sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) to be universal strict epimorphic, it is necessary and sufficient that for every object \(Y \to X\) of \(C\) over \(X\), and for every object \(Z\) of \(C\), the map: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_C(Y,Z) \longrightarrow \varprojlim_{\widehat{C}/(Y \times_X R)} \mathrm{Hom}_C(\,\cdot\,, Z) \] be a bijection.
Proof. Immediate by applying 2.2 then (I 5.3).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 2.7

1) Proposition 2.6 gives a characterization of the universal strict epimorphic sieves of a category \(C\), independent of the universe in which the presheaves take their values, on the sole condition that the sets of morphisms \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\) of \(C\) belong to this universe. It thus allows one to define the canonical topology for every category \(C\), without its being necessary for that to specify the universes.

2) Let \(C\) be a site whose underlying category is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(F\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf, and \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\). The category underlying \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-category, and \(F\) may be regarded as a \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf. The \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf \(F\) is a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf) if and only if the \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf \(F\) is a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf). In other words, the condition for a presheaf \(F\) to be a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf) does not depend (in the sense just made precise) on the universe in which the presheaf \(F\) takes its values. In particular, let \(C\) be a site and \(F\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf; one says that \(F\) is a sheaf (resp. a separated presheaf) if there exists a universe \(\mathcal{V}\) containing \(\mathcal{U}\) such that the category \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-category and such that \(F\) is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaf (resp. a separated \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf). This property does not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{V}\).

footnotes.html: (1) or \(C^{\sim}\), according to the mood of the typewriter.

blocks.html: 3. Sheaf associated to a presheaf

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.0.1

Let \(C\) be a site. A topologically generating family (or, when no confusion results, generating family) of \(C\) is a set \(G\) of objects of \(C\) such that every object of \(C\) is the target of a covering family of morphisms of \(C\) (1.2) whose sources are elements of \(G\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.0.2

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. A \(\mathcal{U}\)-site is a site \(C\) whose underlying category is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category (I 1.1), and which possesses a small topologically generating family. Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category; a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology on \(C\) is a topology on \(C\) making \(C\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. A site \(C\) is said to be \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, or by abuse of language, small, if the category underlying \(C\) is small (I 1.0).
It follows immediately from the definitions that every topology finer than a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology, and that a small site is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.0.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, and \(G\) a small topologically generating family of \(C\). For every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), denote by \(J_G(X)\) the set of sieves covering \(X\) generated by a family of morphisms \((Y_\alpha \xrightarrow{\ u_\alpha\ } X)\), \(\alpha \in A\), where \(Y_\alpha \in G\).

1) The set \(J_G(X)\) is small.

2) The set \(J_G(X)\) is cofinal in the set \(J(X)\) of all the sieves covering \(X\), ordered by inclusion.

3) For every \(R \in J_G(X)\), there exists a small epimorphic family (I 10.2) \((u_\alpha : Y \to R)\), \(\alpha \in A\), with \(Y \in G\).
Proof. 1) Set \(A(X) = \coprod_{Y \in G} \mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)\). The set \(A(X)\) is small (I 0) and \(\mathrm{card}(J_G(X)) \leq 2^{\mathrm{card}(A(X))}\). Consequently \(J_G(X)\) is small.

2) Let \(R \in J(X)\). Set \(A(R) = \coprod_{Y \in G} \mathrm{Hom}(Y,R)\) and let \(R'\) be the sieve of \(X\) generated by the family \((Y \xrightarrow{\ u\ } R \hookrightarrow X)\), \(u \in A(R)\). One has \(R' \subset R\) and it suffices to show that \(R'\) is covering. By axiom (T2) of 1.1, it suffices to show that for every morphism \(Z \to R\), \(Z \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the sieve \(R' \times_X Z\) of \(Z\) is covering. Now the sieve \(R' \times_X Z\) contains the sieve generated by the family of all the morphisms \(Y \to Z\) with \(Y \in G\), a family which is, by hypothesis, covering. The sieve \(R' \times_X Z\) of \(Z\) is therefore covering (axiom T2 of 1.1).

3) Let \(R \in J_G(X)\). The family \((Y \xrightarrow{\ u\ } R)\), \(u \in A(R) = \coprod_{Y \in G} \mathrm{Hom}(Y,R)\) is, by hypothesis, epimorphic. Now, for every \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), \(\mathrm{Hom}(Y,R)\) is contained in \(\mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)\) which is small. Consequently \(A(R)\) is small.

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe such that \(C \in \mathcal{V}\) and \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\), and \(G\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small topologically generating family of \(C\). The category \(\widehat{C}\) of presheaves of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets on \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-category (I 1.1.1). Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\). The set \(J(X)\) of sieves covering \(X\) is \(\mathcal{V}\)-small and, ordered by inclusion, it is cofiltered (1.1.1). For every \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf \(F\), the inductive limit \(\varinjlim_{J(X)} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F)\) is therefore representable by an element of \(\mathcal{V}\) (I 2.4.1). Moreover, it follows from (3.0.4 3)) that, for every \(R \in J_G(X)\), \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F)\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, and since \(J_G(X)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small set cofinal in \(J(X)\) (loc. cit.), it follows from (I 2.4.2) that \(\varinjlim \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F)\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. Let us then choose, for every \(F\) and every \(X\), an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) that represents this inductive limit and set \[ LF(X) = \varinjlim_{J(X)} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(\,\cdot\,, F) . \] Let \(g : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(C\). The base-change functor \(g^* : J(X) \to J(Y)\) defines a map: \[ LF(g) : LF(X) \longrightarrow LF(Y) \] which makes \(X \mapsto LF(X)\) a presheaf on \(C\).

Since the morphism \(\mathrm{id}_X : X \to X\) is an element of \(J(X)\), one has, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), a map: \[ \ell(F)(X) : F(X) \longrightarrow LF(X), \] visibly defining a morphism of functors: \[ \ell(F) : F \longrightarrow LF . \] It is moreover clear that \(F \mapsto LF\) is a functor in \(F\) and that the morphisms \(\ell(F)\) define a morphism \[ \ell : \mathrm{Id} \longrightarrow L . \] Finally, let \(R \hookrightarrow X\) be a refinement of \(X\). The definition of \(LF(X)\) and (I 1.4) furnish us a map: \[ Z_R : \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,LF) , \] and for every morphism of \(C\), \(Y \xrightarrow{\ g\ } X\), the definition of the functor \(LF\) shows us that the diagram below is commutative: \[ (*) \qquad \xymatrix{ Z_R : \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,LF) \ar[d] \\ Z_{R \times_X Y} : \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R \times_X Y, F) \ar[r] & \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,LF) } \] (the vertical arrows are the evident arrows).
Let us then copy [2].

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1

1) For every refinement \(i_R : R \hookrightarrow X\) and every \(u : R \to F\), the diagram: \[ (**) \qquad \xymatrix{ F \ar[r]^-{\ell(F)} & LF \\ R \ar[u]^-{u} \ar[r]_-{i_R} & X \ar[u]_-{Z_R(u)} } \] is commutative.

2) For every morphism \(v : X \to LF\), there exist a refinement \(R\) of \(X\) and a morphism \(u : R \to F\) such that \(Z_R(u) = v\).

3) Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C\) and \(u, v : Y \rightrightarrows F\) two morphisms such that \(\ell(F) \circ u = \ell(F) \circ v\). Then the kernel of the pair \((u,v)\) is a refinement of \(Y\).

4) Let \(R\) and \(R'\) be two refinements of \(X\), \(u : R \to F\) and \(u' : R' \to F\) two morphisms. For \(Z_R(u) = Z_{R'}(u')\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(u\) and \(u'\) coincide on a refinement \(R'' \to R \times_X R'\).

Proof. The only non-trivial assertion is assertion 1). One must show that \(Z_R(u) \circ i_R = \ell(F) \circ u\). For this it suffices to show (I 3.4) that the composites of these morphisms with every morphism \(Y \xrightarrow{\ g\ } R\) (\(Y\) an object of \(C\)) are equal. Now, consider \(f = i_R \circ g\) and the fibre product \(R \times_X Y\): \[ \xymatrix{ F \ar[r]^-{\ell(F)} & LF \\ R \ar[u]^-{u} \ar[r]^-{T_R} & X \ar[u]_-{Z_R(u)} \\ R \times_X Y \ar[u]^-{g'} \ar[r]_-{i'}^-{\sim} & Y \ar[u]_-{f} } \] In this diagram above, \(i'\) is a monomorphism which admits a section. Consequently (1.3.3) \(i'\) is an isomorphism. Now by definition of the morphism \(\ell(F)\), the morphism \(Z_{R \times_X Y}(u \circ g')\) is equal to \(\ell(F) \circ u \circ g\). On the other hand, the commutativity of the diagram (*) furnishes us the equality \(Z_{R \times_X Y}(u \circ g') = Z_R(u) \circ f\), and consequently one indeed has the equality \(\ell(F) \circ u \circ g = Z_R(u) \circ i_R \circ g\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2

1) The functor \(L\) is left exact (I 2.3.2).

2) For every presheaf \(F\), \(LF\) is a separated presheaf.

3) The presheaf \(F\) is separated if and only if the morphism \(\ell(F) : F \to LF\) is a monomorphism. The presheaf \(LF\) is then a sheaf.

4) The following properties are equivalent:

i) \(\ell(F) : F \to LF\) is an isomorphism.

ii) \(F\) is a sheaf.
Proof

1) It suffices to show (I 3.1) that for every object \(X\) of \(C\), the functor \(F \mapsto LF(X)\) commutes with finite projective limits. Now by definition of the projective limit, the functor \[ F \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F) \qquad R \hookrightarrow X \in \mathrm{ob}(J(X)) \] commutes with projective limits, and the inductive limit \(\varinjlim_{J(X)}\) commutes with finite projective limits because \(J(X)\) is a cofiltered set (I 2.7).

2) Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and \(f, g : X \rightrightarrows LF\) two morphisms which coincide on a refinement \(R \hookrightarrow X\) of \(X\). By virtue of 3.1 2), there exist a covering sieve \(R' \hookrightarrow X\), which one may always suppose contained in \(R\), and two morphisms \(u, v : R' \rightrightarrows F\) such that \(Z_{R'}(u) = f\) and \(Z_{R'}(v) = g\). By virtue of 3.1 1) one then has \(\ell(F) \circ u = \ell(F) \circ v\). Consequently (3.1 4)) \(u\) and \(v\) coincide on a refinement \(R'' \hookrightarrow R'\). Let \(w\) be the restriction of \(u\) to \(R''\). One has \(Z_{R''}(w) = Z_{R'}(u) = Z_{R'}(v)\) and consequently \(f = g\). The presheaf \(LF\) is therefore separated.

3) If \(F\) is separated, the morphism \(\ell(F)\) is a monomorphism, because a filtered inductive limit of monomorphisms is a monomorphism. If \(\ell(F)\) is a monomorphism, the presheaf \(F\) is a subpresheaf of a separated presheaf, hence it is separated. Let us show that \(LF\) is then a sheaf. Let \(i : R \hookrightarrow X\) be a sieve covering an object \(X\) of \(C\), and \(u : R \to LF\) a morphism. It suffices for us to show that \(u\) factors through \(X\). Set \(R' = F \times_{LF} R\) and \(v = Z_{R'}(\mathrm{pr}_1)\): \[ \xymatrix{ F \ar[r]^-{\ell(F)} & LF & \\ R' \ar[u]^-{\mathrm{pr}_1} \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{pr}_2} & R \ar[u]^-{u} \ar[r]^-{i} & X \ar[ul]_-{v} \\ R'' \ar[u]^-{p_1} \ar[r]^-{p_2} & Y \ar[u]^-{m} & } \] To show that \(u = v \circ i\), it suffices to show (I 3.4) that for every morphism \(m : Y \to R\) (\(Y\) an object of \(C\)), \(v \circ i \circ m = u \circ m\). Set \(R'' = Y \times_R R'\) and let \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) be the projections. The projection \(R'' \xrightarrow{\ p_2\ } Y\) is a monomorphism and makes \(R''\) a sieve covering \(Y\) (3.1.2)). One has \(v \circ i \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 = \ell(F) \circ \mathrm{pr}_1\) (3.1 1)), and consequently \(v \circ i \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 = u \circ \mathrm{pr}_2\). One deduces \(v \circ i \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ p_1 = u \circ \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ p_1\), i.e. \(v \circ i \circ m \circ p_2 = u \circ m \circ p_2\). Since the presheaf \(LF\) is separated, one has \(v \circ i \circ m = u \circ m\), q.e.d.
4) Clear.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.3

Let \(J'(X)\) be a cofinal subset of \(J(X)\). One has \[ LF(X) = \varinjlim_{J'(X)} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(\,\cdot\,, F) . \] In particular, if the topology of \(C\) is defined by a pretopology \(X \mapsto \mathrm{Cov}(X)\) (1.1.3), the functor \(L\) can be described by means of the covering families of \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) (I 2.12 and I 3.5). On making the formulas explicit one recovers the construction of [1].

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. The inclusion functor \(i : \widetilde{C} \hookrightarrow \widehat{C}\) of sheaves into presheaves admits a left adjoint \(a\), left exact (I 2.3.2): \[ \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C} \ar@{^{(}->}@<-0.7ex>[r]_-{i} & \widehat{C} \ar@<-0.7ex>[l]_-{a} } \] The functor \(i \circ a\) is canonically isomorphic to the functor \(L \circ L\) (cf. 3.0.5). For every presheaf \(F\) the adjunction morphism \(F \to i \circ a(F)\) is deduced, by the preceding isomorphism, from the morphism \(\ell(LF) \circ \ell(F) : F \longrightarrow L \circ L(F)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.5

The sheaf \(aF\) is called the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(F\).
Theorem 3.4 follows immediately from proposition 3.2.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(\mathcal{V} \supset \mathcal{U}\) a universe. Denote by \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) and \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\)) the categories of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves and of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves (resp. of \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves and of \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves) and \(a_{\mathcal{U}} : \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \to \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(a_{\mathcal{V}} : \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \to \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\)) the corresponding "associated sheaf" functors. The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[r]^-{a_{\mathcal{U}}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] & \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] \\ \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \ar[r]^-{a_{\mathcal{V}}} & \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}} } \] where the vertical functors are the canonical inclusions, is commutative up to canonical isomorphism.
Proof. Follows from the construction of the functors \(a_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(a_{\mathcal{V}}\) (3.4 and 3.0.5).

pages.title: 4. Exactness properties of the category of sheaves

blocks.html: 4. Exactness properties of the category of sheaves

The exactness properties of the category of sheaves are deduced from the exactness properties of the category of presheaves via theorem 3.4. The present section makes this philosophy explicit on some of the most useful type-statements.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(\widetilde{C}\) the category of sheaves, \(a : \widehat{C} \to \widetilde{C}\) the associated sheaf functor, and \(i : \widetilde{C} \to \widehat{C}\) the inclusion functor.

1) The functor \(a\) commutes with inductive limits and is exact.

2) The \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive limits in \(\widetilde{C}\) are representable. For every small category \(I\) and every functor \(E : I \to \widetilde{C}\), the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim_I E \longrightarrow a(\varinjlim_I i \circ E) \] is an isomorphism.

3) The \(\mathcal{U}\)-projective limits in \(\widetilde{C}\) are representable. For every object \(X\) of \(C\), the functor on \(\widetilde{C}\): \(F \mapsto F(X)\) commutes with projective limits, i.e. the inclusion functor \(i : \widetilde{C} \to \widehat{C}\) commutes with projective limits.
Proof. These properties follow essentially from theorem 3.4 and from (I 2.11).

Thus, in the category of sheaves, the products indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), fibre products, sums indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), amalgamated sums, kernels, cokernels, images, coimages are representable.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.1.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(F\) a sheaf of sets on \(C\). The canonical homomorphism \[ \varinjlim_{C/F} aX \longrightarrow F \] is an isomorphism.
Proof. Follows from (I 3.4) and from the fact that \(a\) commutes with inductive limits.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2

Every morphism of \(\widetilde{C}\) which is at the same time an epimorphism and a monomorphism is an isomorphism.

Proof. Let \(u : G \to H\) be a morphism of \(\widetilde{C}\) which is an epimorphism and a monomorphism. Let us first remark that the morphism \(u\) is a monomorphism of presheaves (4.1 1)). Let us construct the amalgamated sum \(H \coprod_G H = K\) and the two canonical morphisms \(i_1, i_2 : H \rightrightarrows K\) in the category of presheaves. Since \(u\) is a monomorphism of presheaves, one verifies immediately that the diagram below is cartesian and cocartesian (I 10.1): \[ \xymatrix{ G \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{u} & H \ar[d]^-{i_2} \\ H \ar[r]_-{i_1} & K } \] On applying the "associated sheaf" functor, one therefore obtains a cartesian and cocartesian diagram of the category of sheaves (4.1 1)): \[ (*) \qquad \xymatrix{ G \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{u} & H \ar[d]^-{a i_2} \\ H \ar[r]_-{a i_1} & aK } \] Since \(u\) is an epimorphism of sheaves, the morphism \(a i_1\) is an isomorphism and since the diagram (*) is cartesian, the morphism \(u\) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3

1) The inductive limits in \(\widetilde{C}\) that are representable are universal (I 2.5).

2) Every epimorphic family (I 10.2) of morphisms is universal effective epimorphic (2.6).

3) Every equivalence relation is universal effective (I 10.6).

4) The filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive limits commute with finite projective limits (I 2.6).

Proof. The assertions 1) to 4) are true in the category of sets, hence in the category of presheaves (I 3.1). The assertions 1) and 4) then follow immediately from the corresponding assertions for presheaves and from 4.1. Let us prove 3). Let \(p_1, p_2 : R \rightrightarrows X\) be an equivalence relation of \(\widetilde{C}\). The diagram \(R \rightrightarrows X\) is then an equivalence relation of presheaves (4.1 1)). There therefore exists a morphism of presheaves \(u : X \to Y\) such that the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ R \ar[r]^-{p_2} \ar[d]_-{p_1} & X \ar[d]^-{u} \\ X \ar[r]_-{u} & Y } \] is cartesian and cocartesian in the category of presheaves. On applying the "associated sheaf" functor, one obtains a cartesian and cocartesian diagram in the category of sheaves (4.1 1)). Consequently \(R \rightrightarrows X\) is an effective equivalence relation. Since every equivalence relation is effective by what precedes, every equivalence relation is universal effective. Let us prove 2). Let \((u_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), be an epimorphic family of \(\widetilde{C}\). By (II 2.6) and (I 2.12), it suffices to prove the following assertions:
a) For every morphism of sheaves \(v : Y \to X\), the family of morphisms \(\mathrm{pr}_{2,i} : X_i \times_X Y \to Y\), \(i \in I\), is an epimorphic family of \(\widetilde{C}\).

b) For every sheaf \(Z\) the diagram of sets: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,Z) \longrightarrow \prod_{i \in I} \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,Z) \rightrightarrows \coprod_{(i,k) \in I \times I} \mathrm{Hom}(X_i \times_X X_k, Z) \] is exact.

Let \(X'\) be the union of the images of the morphisms \(u_i\) in the sense of presheaves and \(j : X' \hookrightarrow X\) the canonical injection. For every \(i \in I\), the morphism \(u_i : X_i \to X\) factors into a morphism \(u'_i : X_i \to X'\) and the morphism \(j\), and the family \(u'_i : X_i \to X'\), \(i \in I\), is an epimorphic family of \(\widehat{C}\). Since \(j\) is a monomorphism, the morphism \(aj : aX' \to X\) is a monomorphism of sheaves (4.1). Since for every \(i \in I\), one has \(u_i = aj \circ au'_i\), \(aj\) is an epimorphism of sheaves. Consequently \(aj\) is an isomorphism (4.2). Let \(v : Y \to X\) be a morphism of sheaves. One deduces from it by base change a morphism \(j_v : X' \times_X Y \to Y\) and morphisms \(u'_{i,v} : X_i \times_X Y \to X' \times_X Y\). Since \(a\) commutes with fibre products, \(aj_v\) is an isomorphism. Since the epimorphic families of \(\widehat{C}\) preserve this character under base change, the family \(u'_{i,v}\), \(i \in I\), is epimorphic in \(\widehat{C}\). Since \(a\) commutes with inductive limits, the family \(au'_{i,v} : X_i \times_X Y \longrightarrow a(X' \times_X Y)\), \(i \in I\), is epimorphic in \(\widetilde{C}\), whence a). Let us prove b). Let \(Z\) be a sheaf. Since \(aj\) is an isomorphism, the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,Z) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(X',Z) \] is a bijection. Since the \(u'_i\), \(i \in I\), form an epimorphic family of \(\widehat{C}\), the diagram of sets: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X',Z) \longrightarrow \prod_{i \in I} \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,Z) \rightrightarrows \coprod_{(i,k) \in I \times I} \mathrm{Hom}(X_i \times_X X_k, Z) \] is exact. Finally, since \(X'\) is a subpresheaf of \(X\), the presheaf \(X_i \times_{X'} X_k\), \((i,k) \in I \times I\), is canonically isomorphic to \(X_i \times_X X_k\), whence b).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 4.3.1

1) Proposition 4.3 2) furnishes us formally a second proof of 4.2: It is clear that, in every category, a morphism which is at the same time a universal effective epimorphism and a monomorphism is in fact an isomorphism.

2) One deduces from the preceding propositions that every morphism in the category of sheaves factors in a unique way into an effective epimorphism and an effective monomorphism. This property generalizes in a natural way, for non-additive categories, the axiom (AB2) of abelian categories (\(\mathrm{coim} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{im}\)) [Tohoku].

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. The functor \(h : C \to \widehat{C}\) (I 1.3.1), composed with the associated sheaf functor, furnishes a functor \[ \varepsilon_C : C \longrightarrow \widetilde{C} , \] called the canonical functor of \(C\) into \(\widetilde{C}\), which will be constantly used in the sequel. The functor \(\varepsilon_C\) commutes with finite projective limits. When the topology of \(C\) is less fine than the canonical topology, \(\varepsilon_C\) is fully faithful, and commutes with projective limits; it is then, moreover, defined when \(C\) does not necessarily possess a small topologically generating family. We shall not study in detail the behaviour of \(\varepsilon_C\) with respect to inductive limits (cf. [SGA 3 IV]). We shall however need the following propositions.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \((u_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), a family of morphisms of \(C\) with target \(X\). The following conditions are equivalent (∗):

i) The family \((\varepsilon_C u_i : \varepsilon_C X_i \longrightarrow \varepsilon_C X)\), \(i \in I\), is an epimorphic family of \(\widetilde{C}\) (I 10.2).

ii) The family \((u_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), is a covering family of \(C\) (1.2).

Proof. ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). Let \(R \hookrightarrow X\) be the sieve generated by the \(u_i\), \(i \in I\) (I 4.3.3), and \(u'_i : X_i \to R\) the morphisms induced by the \(u_i\). The family of the \(u'_i\), \(i \in I\), is a family epimorphic in \(\widehat{C}\), and \(R\) is a sieve covering \(X\). Consequently, for every sheaf \(F\), the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(R,F) \] is bijective and the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(R,F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,F) \] is injective. Hence the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,F) \] is injective and consequently the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(aX,F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(aX_i,F) \] is injective, whence i).

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). With the notations introduced previously, let \(J_R : R \hookrightarrow X\) be the canonical injection into \(X\) of the sieve generated by the \(u_i\), \(i \in I\). It follows from i) that the morphism of sheaves \(aJ_R : aR \to aX\) is at the same time an epimorphism of sheaves and a monomorphism of sheaves. It is therefore an isomorphism of sheaves (4.2). One has, with the notations of n° 3, a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[r]^-{\ell(X)} & LX \ar[r]^-{\ell(LX)} & aX \\ R \ar[u]^-{J_R} \ar[r]_-{\ell(R)} & LR \ar[u]^-{LJ_R} \ar[r]_-{\ell(LR)} & aR \ar[u]_-{aJ_R}^-{\wr} } \] First of all, by 3.1 2), there exist a covering sieve \(J_{S_1} : S_1 \hookrightarrow X\) and a morphism \(u_1 : S_1 \to LR\) such that \[ (4.6.1) \qquad \ell(LX) \circ \ell(X) \circ J_{S_1} = aJ_R \circ \ell(LR) \circ u_1 = \ell(LX) \circ LJ_R \circ u_1 . \] Set \(m = \ell(X) \circ J_{S_1}\) and \(n = LJ_R \circ u_1\). The morphisms \(m\) and \(n\) are morphisms from \(S_1\) into \(LX\). Let \(S_2 \hookrightarrow S_1\) be the kernel of the pair of arrows \((m,n)\). For every object \(Y\) of \(C\) and every morphism \(\alpha : Y \to S_1\), one has, by virtue of (4.6.1), \(\ell(LX) \circ m \circ \alpha = \ell(LX) \circ n \circ \alpha\). It then follows from (3.1.3)) that the kernel \(S_2 \times_{S_1} Y\) of the pair of arrows \((m \circ \alpha, n \circ \alpha)\) is a sieve covering \(Y\). Consequently, by axiom (T2) of topologies, \(J_{S_2} : S_2 \hookrightarrow X\) is a sieve covering \(X\). One therefore has a morphism \(u_2 : S_2 \to LR\) and a commutative diagram: \[ (4.6.2) \qquad \xymatrix{ S_2 \ar[rr]^-{J_{S_2}} \ar[dd]_-{u_2} & & X \ar[dd]^-{\ell(X)} \\ & R \ar[ur]_-{J_R} \ar[dl]^-{\ell(R)} & \\ LR \ar[rr]_-{LJ_R} & & LX } \] Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C\) and \(\beta : Y \to S_2\) a morphism. By 3.1 1), there exist a covering sieve \(J_{Q_1} : Q_1 \hookrightarrow Y\) and a morphism \(v_1 : Q_1 \to LR\) such that \(u_2 \circ \beta \circ J_{Q_1} = \ell(R) \circ v_1\). Set \(f = J_{S_2} \circ \beta \circ J_{Q_1}\), \(g = J_R \circ v_1\). Let \(Q_2\) be the kernel of the pair \((f,g) : Q_1 \rightrightarrows X\) and \(J_{Q_2} : Q_2 \hookrightarrow Y\) the canonical injection. For every object \(Z\) of \(C\) and every morphism \(\gamma : Z \to Q_1\), one has, by virtue of the commutativity of (4.6.2): \[ \ell(X) \circ f \circ \gamma = \ell(X) \circ J_{S_2} \circ \beta \circ J_{Q_1} \circ \gamma = LJ_R \circ u_2 \circ \beta \circ J_{Q_1} \circ \gamma = \] \[ = LJ_R \circ \ell(R) \circ v_1 \circ \gamma = \ell(X) \circ J_R \circ v_1 \circ \gamma = \ell(X) \circ g \circ \gamma . \] It then follows from 3.1.2) that the kernel \(Q_2 \times_{Q_1} Z\) of the pair \((f \circ \gamma, g \circ \gamma)\) is a sieve covering \(Z\). By axiom (T 2) of topologies, \(J_{Q_2} : Q_2 \hookrightarrow Y\) is a sieve covering \(Y\). For every morphism \(\beta : Y \to S\), there therefore exist a covering sieve \(J_{Q_2} : Q_2 \hookrightarrow Y\) and a morphism \(v_2 : Q_2 \to R\) such that the diagram below is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ Y \ar[r]^-{\beta} & S_2 \ar[r]^-{J_{S_2}} & X \\ Q_2 \ar[u]^-{J_{Q_2}} \ar[rr]_-{v_2} & & R \ar[u]_-{J_R} } \] Denote then by \(S_2 \cap R\) the fibre product of \(S_2\) and \(R\) over \(X\). The sieve (of \(Y\)): \((S_2 \cap R) \times_{S_2} Y\) contains the sieve \(Q_2\) and consequently \((S_2 \cap R) \times_{S_2} Y\) is a sieve covering \(Y\). It then follows from axiom (T 2) of topologies that \(S_2 \cap R\) is a sieve covering \(X\) and consequently the sieve \(R\) which contains \(S_2 \cap R\) is a sieve covering \(X\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4.4

Let \(T\) be the topology of the \(\mathcal{U}\)-site \(C\), and \(T'\) (resp. \(T''\)) the finest topology on \(C\) among those for which the objects of \(\widetilde{C}\) are sheaves (resp. presheaves) (2.2). Then \(T = T' = T''\).
Indeed, one has trivially \(T \leq T' \leq T''\), and 4.4 and 2.2 imply that \(T'' \leq T\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.5

An initial object of a category \(A\) is an object \(\varnothing_A\) which represents the empty inductive limit, i.e. such that for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, A\), there exists one and only one arrow \(\varnothing_A \to X\). An object \(\varnothing_A\) is said to be strict initial if it is initial and if every morphism with target \(\varnothing_A\) is an isomorphism. Let \((S_i)\), \(i \in I\), be a family of objects of a category \(A\). Suppose that the sum \(s = \coprod_{i \in I} S_i\) is representable. The sum \(S\) is said to be disjoint if the structural morphisms \(S_i \to S\) are squarable, if they are monomorphisms and if for every pair \(i,j\), \(i \neq j\) the product \(S_i \times_S S_j\) is an initial object of \(A\). The sum \(S\) is said to be universal disjoint if it is disjoint and if it remains a disjoint sum after every base change \(T \to S\); it follows that for every pair \(i,j\), \(i \neq j\), the objects \(S_i \times_S S_j\) are strict initial objects of \(A\).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 4.5.1

In the category of sets, direct sums are disjoint and universal. The same therefore holds in every category of presheaves of sets (I 3.1) and consequently in every category of sheaves of sets on a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (4.1); in particular, the initial object of \(\widetilde{C}\) is strict.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.6

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and \((s_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), a family of morphisms of \(C\). For every \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology \(\mathscr{C}\) on \(C\) (3.0.2), denote by \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathscr{C}}\) the category of corresponding sheaves and by \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}} : C \to \widetilde{C}_{\mathscr{C}}\) the corresponding functor.

1) Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology such that \[ \coprod_{i \in I} \varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X_i) \xrightarrow{\ (\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(s_i))\ } \varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X) \] is an isomorphism. Then for every topology \(\mathscr{C}'\) finer than \(\mathscr{C}\), the morphism: \[ \coprod_{i \in I} \varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}'}(X_i) \xrightarrow{\ (\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}'}(s_i))\ } \varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}'}(X) \] is an isomorphism.

2) Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology on \(C\). The following properties (i) and (ii) are equivalent:

i) a) The family \((s_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), is covering for \(\mathscr{C}\).

b) For every \(i \in I\), the diagonal morphism of presheaves \(\Delta_i : X_i \hookrightarrow X_i \times_X X_i\) is transformed by the "associated sheaf" functor (for \(\mathscr{C}\)) into an isomorphism (which is the case if the \(s_i\) are monomorphisms).

c) For every pair \((i,j)\), \(i \neq j\), of elements of \(I\), the presheaf \(X_i \times_X X_j\) is transformed by the "associated sheaf" functor (for \(\mathscr{C}\)) into the initial object of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathscr{C}}\).

ii) \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X)\) is a sum of the \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X_i)\).
Proof.

1) A sheaf \(F\) for \(\mathscr{C}'\) is a sheaf for \(\mathscr{C}\). Consequently, for every sheaf \(F\) for \(\mathscr{C}'\), the morphism \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X,F) \longrightarrow \prod_{i \in I} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(X_i,F) \] is an isomorphism, which entails the assertion.

2) By definition, one has property ii) if and only if the morphism of presheaves \[ \Phi = (h(s_i), i \in I) : \coprod_i h(X_i) \longrightarrow h(X) \] is transformed by the "associated sheaf" functor into an isomorphism, i.e. (4.2) if and only if \(a(\Phi)\) is an epimorphism and monomorphism of sheaves. By (4.4), the morphism \(a(\Phi)\) is an epimorphism if and only if one has property a). The diagonal morphism \[ \Delta : \coprod_i h(X_i) \longrightarrow \Bigl(\coprod_i h(X_i)\Bigr) \times_{h(X)} \Bigl(\coprod_i h(X_i)\Bigr) \] is the direct sum of a family \(\Delta_{i,j}\), \((i,j) \in I \times I\), of morphisms defined as follows:
β) When \(i = j\), \(\Delta_{i,i}\) is the diagonal morphism \(h(X_i) \to h(X_i) \times_{h(X)} h(X_i)\).
γ) When \(i \neq j\), \(\Delta_{i,j}\) is the morphism \(\varnothing_{\widehat{C}} \to h(X_i) \times_{h(X)} h(X_j)\) (\(\varnothing_{\widehat{C}}\) denotes the initial object of \(\widehat{C}\)).

The morphism \(a(\Phi)\) is a monomorphism if and only if \(a(\Delta)\) is an isomorphism, and by (4.1) \(a(\Delta)\) is an isomorphism if and only if the \(a(\Delta_{i,j})\) are isomorphisms, i.e. if and only if one has properties b) and c).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.6.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and \(X\) an object of \(C\).

1) Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology on \(C\). The object \(X\) of \(C\) is transformed by the "associated sheaf" functor (for the topology \(\mathscr{C}\)) into the initial object of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathscr{C}}\) if and only if the empty sieve covers \(X\).

2) When \(X\) is a strict initial object of \(C\), the sheaf associated to \(X\), for every \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology finer than the canonical topology, is an initial object.
Proof.
1) One takes for the set \(I\) in 4.6 2) the empty set.

2) By 1) and 4.6 1), it suffices to show that the empty sieve covers \(X\) for the canonical topology, i.e. (2.6) it suffices to show that for every object \(Y \to X\) over \(X\), \(Y\) is an initial object of \(X\), which follows from the definition (4.5).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.6.2

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \((s_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), a family of squarable morphisms of \(C\) with the same target, possessing the following properties:

α) The family of the \(s_i\), \(i \in I\), is covering.

β) For every \(i \in I\), \(s_i : X_i \to X\) is a monomorphism.

γ) For every pair \((i,j)\), \(i \neq j\), of elements of \(I\), \(X_i \times_X X_j\) is covered by the empty sieve, i.e. for every sheaf \(F\) on \(C\), \(F(X_i \times_X X_j)\) is a set reduced to one element.

Then \(\varepsilon_C(X)\) is the sum of the \(\varepsilon_C(X_i)\), \(i \in I\).
Proof. Follows immediately from 4.6 2) and from 4.6.1 1).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.6.3

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and \((s_i : X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), a family of squarable morphisms with the same target. Suppose that the canonical topology of \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology. The following conditions are equivalent:

i) There exists a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology \(\mathscr{C}\) on \(C\), less fine than the canonical topology, such that \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X)\) is the sum of the \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X_i)\), \(i \in I\).

ii) The object \(X\) is the disjoint and universal sum (4.5) (in \(C\)) of the \(X_i\).

Proof. ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). Since \(X\) is the universal sum of the \(X_i\), \(i \in I\), the family of the \(s_i\), \(i \in I\), is covering for the canonical topology of \(C\) (2.6). Condition α) of 4.6.2 is therefore satisfied when one equips \(C\) with the canonical topology. Condition β) is evidently satisfied and property γ) follows from 4.6.1) 2), whence i).

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a topology on \(C\) less fine than the canonical topology such that \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X)\) is the sum of the \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X_i)\). For every sheaf \(F\), for \(\mathscr{C}\), the canonical map \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,F) \to \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,F)\) is a bijection. Moreover, every representable presheaf is a sheaf. It follows immediately that \(X\) is the sum in \(C\) of the \(X_i\), \(i \in I\). Applying this to the case where the set \(I\) is empty, one sees that if an object of \(C\) is transformed into the initial object of \(\widetilde{C}\), this object is an initial object of \(C\). The functor \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) is fully faithful and commutes with finite projective limits. Consequently condition b) of 4.6 2) entails that the \(s_i\), \(i \in I\), are monomorphisms of \(C\), and condition c) entails, by what precedes, that the \(X_i \times_X X_j\), \(i \neq j\), are initial objects of \(C\). Consequently \(X\) is the disjoint sum of the \(X_i\). Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}\) commutes with fibre products, this last property is stable under every base change \(Y \to X\), and consequently \(X\) is the disjoint and universal sum of the \(X_i\), \(i \in I\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.6.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and \(X\) an object of \(C\). Suppose that the canonical topology on \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology. The following properties are equivalent:

i) There exists on \(C\) a topology less fine than the canonical topology such that \(\varepsilon_{\mathscr{C}}(X)\) is an initial object of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathscr{C}}\).

ii) \(X\) is a strict initial object of \(C\).
Proof. One takes for the set \(I\) the empty set in 4.6.3 .

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.7

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(\widetilde{C}\) the category of sheaves on \(C\) for the canonical topology, \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) the canonical functor (4.4.0), \(R \rightrightarrows X\) an equivalence relation in \(C\) admitting a cokernel \(Y\) in \(C\). Let \(\pi : X \to Y\) be the morphism canonical and suppose it squarable. Consider then the following properties:

i) \(\varepsilon_C(Y)\) is the quotient of the equivalence relation \(\varepsilon_C(R) \rightrightarrows \varepsilon_C(X)\).

ii) The equivalence relation \(R \rightrightarrows X\) is universal effective (cf. n° 7).

One has ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). When \(C\) possesses a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology less fine than the canonical topology, one has i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii).

Proof. ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). The canonical morphism \(R \to X \times_Y X\) is an isomorphism. Let \(S \hookrightarrow Y\) be the sieve generated by \(\pi : X \to Y\). For every presheaf \(F\), one has an exact diagram (I 2.12): \[ \mathrm{Hom}(S,F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(X,F) \rightrightarrows \mathrm{Hom}(R,F) . \] It therefore suffices to show that for every sheaf \(F\) for the canonical topology, the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(S,F) \] is a bijection, i.e. it suffices to show that \(S\) is covering for the canonical topology, or again that the sieve generated by \(\pi : X \to Y\) is covering, which follows from definition 2.5.

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). The functor \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) commutes with finite projective limits and is fully faithful. Now the canonical morphism \(\varepsilon_C(R) \to \varepsilon_C(X) \times_{\varepsilon_C(Y)} \varepsilon_C(X)\) is an isomorphism (4.3). Consequently the morphism canonical \(R \to X \times_Y X\) is an isomorphism. The morphism \(\varepsilon_C(X) \to \varepsilon_C(Y)\) is an epimorphism, which entails (4.4) that \(\pi : X \to Y\) is a covering morphism of \(C\) for the canonical topology, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.8

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. The category of sheaves on \(C\) possesses the following properties:

a) The finite projective limits are representable.

b) The direct sums indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) are representable. They are disjoint and universal. (4.5)

c) The equivalence relations are universal effective.
This has been seen in 4.1, 2) and 3), 4.3, 3), and 4.5.1.

These properties have been brought out because they will later allow one to characterize the \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories equivalent to categories of sheaves on categories belonging to \(\mathcal{U}\) (IV 1.2).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

Let us recall that property a) is equivalent to the property: there exists a final object, and the fibre products are representable (I 2.3.1).

Let \(C\) be a site whose underlying category is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. Then the category \(\widetilde{C}\) of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves on \(C\) satisfies the conditions envisaged in I 7.3 ((i) or (ii), as one wishes), hence by loc. cit. the various variants envisaged in I 7.1 for the notion of generating family in \(\widetilde{C}\) coincide. This being posited:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.10

With the preceding notations, consider the functor canonical \(\varepsilon : C \to \widetilde{C}\) (4.4.0), and let \(G \subset \mathrm{ob}\, C\) be a topologically generating family in \(C\) (3.0.1). Then the family \((\varepsilon(X))_{X \in G}\) of objects of \(\widetilde{C}\) is a generating family. In particular the family \((\varepsilon(X))_{X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C}\) of objects of \(C\) is generating.

One must prove that every morphism \(u : F \to F'\) in \(\widetilde{C}\) such that \[ (4.10.1) \qquad \mathrm{Hom}(\varepsilon(X),F) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(\varepsilon(X),F') \] is a bijection for every \(X \in G\), is an isomorphism. Now the preceding map is identified with the map \[ (4.10.2) \qquad u(X) : F(X) \longrightarrow F'(X) , \] and one must show that if this is bijective for every \(X \in G\), the same holds for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\). Now let \((X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) be a family covering \(X\) by objects of \(G\), and for every pair of indices \((i,j)\) of \(I\), consider the set of all the morphisms \(X_{ijk} \to X_i \times_X X_j\) in \(\widetilde{C}\), with \(X_{ijk} \in G\) (\(k\) ranging over an index set \(I_{i,j}\)). One then obtains a homomorphism of exact diagrams of sets \[ \xymatrix{ F(X) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \prod_i F(X_i) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] \ar[d]^-{\wr} & \prod_{ijk} F(X_{ijk}) \ar[d]^-{\wr} \\ F'(X) \ar[r] & \prod_i F'(X_i) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & \prod_{ijk} F'(X_{ijk}) } \] where by hypothesis the last two vertical arrows are bijections. The same therefore holds for the first vertical arrow, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.11

Suppose that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (3.0.2). Then the category \(\widetilde{C}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and admits a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small generating family.

Indeed, by hypothesis one may take in 4.10 for \(G\) a small generating family, which proves the existence of a small generating family. On the other hand, if \(F, F' \in \mathrm{ob}\, \widetilde{C}\), a homomorphism from \(F\) into \(F'\) is known when one knows the homomorphism (4.10.1) i.e. (4.10.2) for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, G\) (I 7.1.1), whence it follows that the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(F,F') \longrightarrow \prod_{X \in G} \mathrm{Hom}(F(X), F'(X)) \] is injective. Since the second member is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, the same holds for the first, which proves that \(\widetilde{C}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.12

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. Then for every object of \(\widetilde{C}\), the set of subobjects of \(X\) and the set of quotient objects of \(X\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small.
This follows from I 7.4 resp. I 7.5, which apply thanks to 4.11.

footnotes.html: (∗) When the site \(C\) does not necessarily possess a small topologically generating family and when the topology of \(C\) is less fine than the canonical topology, one has ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i) (cf. the proof of 4.4).

pages.title: 5. Extension of a topology of \(C\) to \(\widehat{C}\)

blocks.html: 5. Extension of a topology of \(C\) to \(\widehat{C}\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(f : H \to K\) a morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). The following conditions are equivalent:

i) For every \(X \to K\), with \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the corresponding morphism \(H \times_K X \to X\) has for image a sieve covering \(X\).

ii) The morphism \(a(f) : aH \to aK\) on the associated sheaves is an epimorphism of \(\widetilde{C}\).

ii bis) For every sheaf \(F\) on \(C\), the map \(\mathrm{Hom}(K,F) \to \mathrm{Hom}(H,F)\) deduced from \(f\) is injective.
Proof. It is clear that ii) is equivalent to ii bis).

Let us prove that (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii). By virtue of 4.4, (i) means that \(u : a(H \times_K X) \to a(X)\) is an epimorphism. Now, since \(a(H \times_K X) \simeq a(H) \times_{a(K)} a(X)\), \(a\) commuting with finite \(\varprojlim\) (4.1), the morphism envisaged is deduced from \(a(f) : a(H) \to a(K)\) by base change. Since the epimorphisms of \(\widetilde{C}\) are universal, this shows that (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). Conversely, since the family of the \(X_i \to K\) is epimorphic, the same holds for the family of the \(a(X) \to a(K)\) in \(\widetilde{C}\) (4.1), so to verify that \(a(f) : a(H) \to a(K)\) is epimorphic, it suffices to see it after every base change of the preceding type \(a(X) \to a(K)\), which proves i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.2

1) A morphism \(f : H \to K\) satisfying the three conditions equivalent of 5.1 is called a covering morphism. A family of morphisms \(f_i : H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), with the same target is said to be covering if the corresponding morphism \(f : \coprod_i H_i \to K\) is covering.

2) A morphism \(f : H \to K\) is said to be bicovering if it is covering and if the morphism diagonal \(H \to H \times_K H\) is covering. A family \(f_i : H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), with the same target is said to be bicovering if the corresponding morphism \(f : \coprod_i H_i \to K\) is bicovering.

By condition i) of 5.1, to say that a family \((f_i : H_i \to K)\), \(i \in I\), is covering, means that for every morphism \(X \to K\), with \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the family of the \(H_i \times_K X \to X\), \(i \in I\), has for image a sieve covering \(X\); or again, by ii), the family of morphisms \(a(f_i) : aH_i \to aK\) in \(\widetilde{C}\) is epimorphic (taking into account that the functor \(a\) commutes with direct sums (4.1))(∗).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.3

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(f : H \to K\) a morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). The following conditions are equivalent:

i) The morphism \(f\) is bicovering.

i bis) The morphism \(f\) is covering and for every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every pair of morphisms \(u,v : X \rightrightarrows H\) such that \(fu = fv\), the kernel of \((u,v)\) is a sieve covering \(X\).

ii) The morphism \(a(f) : aH \to aK\) is an isomorphism of \(\widetilde{C}\).

ii bis) For every sheaf \(F\) on \(C\), the map \(\mathrm{Hom}(K,F) \to \mathrm{Hom}(H,F)\) is a bijection.

Proof. The equivalence i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) i bis) follows from condition i) of 5.1, applied to the diagonal morphism \(H \to H \times_K H\); the equivalence ii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) ii bis) is trivial.

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). The morphism \(a(f) : aH \to aK\) is an epimorphism (5.1). Since the functor \(a\) commutes with the formation of fibre products (4.1), the diagonal morphism \(aH \to aH \times_{aK} aH\) is an epimorphism (5.1). Since the diagonal morphism is always a monomorphism, it is an isomorphism (4.2). Consequently the morphism \(a(f)\) is a monomorphism. It is therefore an isomorphism (4.2).

ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). Since the functor \(a\) commutes with the formation of fibre products, the morphism \(f\) and the diagonal morphism \(H \to H \times_K H\) are transformed by \(a\) into isomorphisms. In particular, they are transformed by \(a\) into epimorphisms. They are therefore covering, q.e.d.

It follows from 5.3, and from the fact that \(a\) commutes with direct sums, that a family \((f_i : H_i \to K)\), \(i \in I\), of morphisms of \(\widehat{C}\) is bicovering if and only if the \(f_i\) induce on the associated sheaves an isomorphism from the direct sum \(\coprod_i aH_i\) onto \(aK\), or again if and only if, for every sheaf \(F\), the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(K,F) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(H_i,F) \] is bijective.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. There exists on \(\widehat{C}\) a topology (evidently unique) such that a family \(H_i \to K\) of arrows of \(\widehat{C}\) with the same target is covering for this topology if and only if it is covering in the sense of 5.2. It is also the topology the least fine on \(\widehat{C}\) among the topologies \(T\) having the following properties:

a) \(T\) is finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\) (i.e. every family epimorphic of \(\widehat{C}\) is covering for \(T\)).

b) Every covering family in \(C\) is covering in \(\widehat{C}\).

Proof. We shall limit ourselves to giving indications. We leave to the reader the task of showing that the covering families in the sense of 5.2 are the covering families of a topology \(T_C\) on \(\widehat{C}\) (one uses 4.1). The covering families of the canonical topology on \(\widehat{C}\) are the epimorphic families on \(\widehat{C}\) (2.6 and I 3.1). Since \(a\) commutes with inductive limits (4.1), the topology \(T_C\) is finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\). Moreover the covering families of \(C\) are covering families of \(T_C\) (5.1). If, then, \(T'\) denotes the least fine of the topologies of \(\widehat{C}\) possessing the properties a) and b), \(T_C\) is finer than \(T'\). Let \((f_i : H_i \to K)\), \(i \in I\), be a covering family of \(T_C\). Let us show that \((f_i, i \in I)\) is a family covering of \(T'\). Let \(s_i : H_i \to H = \coprod H_i\) be the canonical monomorphisms and \(f = (f_i, i \in I) : H = \coprod_i H_i \to K\) the morphism defined by the \(f_i\). The family of the \(s_i\) is covering for \(T'\). To show that \((f_i, i \in I)\) is a covering family of \(T'\), it therefore suffices to show, by virtue of axiom (T2) of topologies, that the morphism \(f : H \to K\) is covering for \(T'\). There exists an epimorphic family of \(\widehat{C}\), \(u_\lambda : X_\lambda \to K\), \(\lambda \in \Lambda\), \(X_\lambda \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\) (I 3.4). To show that \(f : H \to K\) is covering for \(T'\), it therefore suffices, by virtue of axiom (T 2) of topologies, to show that for every \(\lambda \in \Lambda\), the morphism \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : H \times_K X_\lambda \to X_\lambda\) is covering for \(T'\). Let then \(v_j : Y_j \to H \times_K X_\lambda\), \(j \in J\), \(Y_j \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), be an epimorphic family of \(\widehat{C}\). The family \((\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ v_j, j \in J)\) is covering for \(T_C\). It is therefore a covering family of \(C\) (5.1). It is therefore a covering family of \(T'\). Consequently the sieve generated by \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : H \times_K X_\lambda \to X_\lambda\) contains a sieve covering for \(T'\). It is therefore covering for \(T'\) and consequently \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : H \times_K X_\lambda \to X_\lambda\) is covering, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.4.1

The proof of 5.4 shows in fact that every topology \(T'\) on \(\widehat{C}\), finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\), is the least fine of the topologies \(T\) on \(\widehat{C}\) that possess the following properties:

a) \(T\) is finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\).

b) Every family covering for \(T'\) of the form \(u_i : X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), where \(X\) and the \(X_i\) are objects of \(C\), is covering for \(T\).

In particular, every topology \(T'\) on \(\widehat{C}\), finer than the canonical topology, is uniquely determined by the families \(u_i : X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), \(X_i\) and \(X\) objects of \(C\), that are covering for \(T'\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.4.2

One can easily show that for every topology \(T'\) on \(\widehat{C}\), finer than the canonical topology, the set of families of morphisms \((X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), with the same target in \(C\), that are covering for \(T'\), is the set of covering families of a topology on \(C\). Thus 5.4 and 5.4.1 allow one to establish a one-to-one correspondence between the topologies on \(C\) and the topologies on \(\widehat{C}\) finer than the canonical topology.

Let \(C\) be a small category. Denote by \(\mathrm{Caf}\) the set of strictly full subcategories (every object isomorphic to an object of the subcategory is an object of the subcategory) of \(\widehat{C}\) whose injection functor admits a left adjoint which commutes with finite projective limits. Denote also by \(\mathscr{T}\) the set of topologies on \(C\). The theorem 3.4 defines for us a map: \[ \Phi : \mathscr{T} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Caf} . \] We are going to define a map in the reverse direction. For this, one must associate to every element \(e = (i' : C' \rightleftarrows \widehat{C}\), \(a'\) a left adjoint of \(i')\) a topology \(T_e\) on \(C\). For every object \(X\) of \(C\), we shall define \(J_e(X)\) as being the set of subobjects of \(X\) whose injection morphism is transformed by \(a'\) into an isomorphism. One verifies immediately, with the help of the hypotheses made on \(a'\), that one thus defines a topology \(T_e\) on \(C\). One has therefore defined a map: \[ \Psi : \mathrm{Caf} \longrightarrow \mathscr{T} . \] One then has the result (due to J. GIRAUD):

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.5

The map \(\Phi\) is a bijection, and \(\Psi\) is the inverse map.

Proof. The map \(\Psi \circ \Phi\) is the identity. Indeed, this follows immediately from 5.1. The map \(\Phi \circ \Psi\) is the identity. Indeed, let \((i' : C' \rightleftarrows \widehat{C})\) be an element of \(\mathrm{Caf}\), \(T_e\) the topology which corresponds to it by \(\Psi\), \(C_e\) the category of sheaves for \(T_e\). One then proves, using the definition of the topology \(T_e\) and the definition of the morphisms bicovering (5.2), the equivalence of the following assertions:
i) The morphism \(u\) of \(\widehat{C}\) is bicovering for the topology \(T_e\).
ii) The morphism \(u\) of \(\widehat{C}\) is transformed by \(a'\) into an isomorphism.

It is clear that \(C'\) is a full subcategory of \(C_e\). It therefore suffices to show that every sheaf \(F\) for the topology \(T_e\) is an object of \(C'\). But, by the equivalence above, the morphism \(F \to i' \circ a'(F)\) is bicovering, and its source and its target being sheaves, one deduces by 5.3 (ii) that \(F \to i' \circ a'(F)\) is an isomorphism, q.e.d.

footnotes.html: (∗) Note that the property for a morphism or a family of morphisms of \(\widehat{C}\) to be covering (resp. bicovering) is stable under base change.

pages.title: 6. Sheaves with values in a category

blocks.html: 6. Sheaves with values in a category
Let \(C\) and \(D\) be two categories. A contravariant functor from \(C\) into \(D\), \(F : C^\circ \to D\), is called a presheaf on \(C\) with values in \(D\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.1

Let \(C\) be a site, \(D\) a category. A presheaf \(F : C^\circ \to D\) is called a sheaf on \(C\) with values in \(D\) (or, more briefly, a sheaf with values in \(D\)) if for every object \(S\) of \(D\), the presheaf of sets: \[ X \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_D(S, F(X)) , \qquad X \in \mathrm{ob}(C) \] is a sheaf. The full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ, D)\) formed of the sheaves on \(C\) with values in \(D\) will be denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}^{\sim}(C^\circ, D)\).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 6.2

1) Condition 6.1 means that for every object \(X\) of \(C\), every covering sieve \(R\) of \(X\), and every object \(S\) of \(D\), one has an isomorphism (I 3.5 and 2.1): \[ \mathrm{Hom}_D(S, F(X)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C/R} F(\,\cdot\,) . \] One thus recovers, when \(D\) is the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets, the definition of sheaves of sets (loc. cit.).

2) Let \(D'\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and \(G : D \to D'\) a functor commuting with projective limits. The functor \(G\) transforms, by composition, the sheaves with values in \(D\) into sheaves with values in \(D'\).

Let \(\gamma\) be a species of algebraic structure defined by finite projective limits (I 2.9) and \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\) the category of \(\gamma\)-sets that belong to \(\mathcal{U}\). Denote by \(\mathrm{esj} : \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) the "underlying set" functor. The functor \(\mathrm{esj}\) commutes with projective limits and, consequently, by the preceding remark, defines by composition functors: \[ \mathrm{esj}^\wedge : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma) \longrightarrow \widehat{C} \] \[ \mathrm{esj}^\sim : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}^{\sim}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma) \longrightarrow \widetilde{C} . \] The functor \(\mathrm{esj}^\sim\) is called the "underlying sheaf of sets" functor. In fact, it factors in a canonical way through the category \(\gamma\text{-}\widetilde{C}\) of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\widetilde{C}\), and, still denoting by \(\widetilde{\mathrm{esj}}\) the functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}^{\sim}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma) \longrightarrow \gamma\text{-}\widetilde{C} \] obtained, one can state:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.3.1

The functor \(\mathrm{esj}^\sim\) establishes an equivalence of categories between the category of sheaves on \(C\) with values in \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\), that of the \(\gamma\)-objects of the category of sheaves of sets, and the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of the category of presheaves of sets whose underlying presheaf is a sheaf.
Proof. The proof uses essentially (I 3.2) and the fact that a finite projective limit of sheaves in the category of presheaves is a sheaf (4.1).

The preceding proposition justifies the abuse of language which consists in identifying a sheaf with values in \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\) and the corresponding \(\gamma\)-object in \(\widetilde{C}\). We shall from now on systematically make this abuse of language. We shall employ the classical terminology: sheaves of groups, sheaves of commutative groups (which we shall most often call abelian sheaves), sheaves of rings, sheaves of \(A\)-modules...

We denote by \[ \widetilde{C}_\gamma \quad (\text{resp. } \widehat{C}_\gamma) \] the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\widetilde{C}\) (resp. of \(\widehat{C}\)). When \(\gamma\) is the species of structure "\(A\)-module", one also writes \(\widetilde{C}_A\), or simply \(\widetilde{C}_{ab}\) when \(A = \mathbb{Z}\).
Suppose that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. The "associated sheaf" functor is left exact (4.1) and consequently:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4

The inclusion functor \(i_\gamma : \widetilde{C}_\gamma \to \widehat{C}_\gamma\) admits a left adjoint \(a_\gamma\), left exact, i.e. one has an isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}_\gamma}(a_\gamma\,,\ ) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}_\gamma}(\ ,\ i_\gamma) . \] Let \(X\) be an object of \(\widehat{C}_\gamma\). The underlying sheaf of sets of \(a_\gamma(X)\) is canonically isomorphic to the sheaf associated to the underlying presheaf of sets of \(X\). The morphism of underlying presheaves of sets of the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id} \to i_\gamma a_\gamma\) is identified with the adjunction morphism applied to the underlying presheaf of sets.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.5

Suppose that the functor \(\mathrm{esj} : \gamma\text{-}\mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) admits a left adjoint(∗): \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}}(.\,, \mathrm{esj}(.)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\gamma\text{-}\mathcal{U}}(\mathrm{Lib}(.),.) . \] The functor \(\mathrm{esj}^\sim : \widetilde{C}_\gamma \to \widetilde{C}\) (resp. \(\mathrm{esj}^\wedge : \widehat{C}_\gamma \to \widehat{C}\)) admits a left adjoint \(\mathrm{Lib}^\sim\) (resp. \(\mathrm{Lib}^\wedge\)) and one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \mathrm{Lib}^\sim = a_\gamma \mathrm{Lib}^\wedge i . \]
Proof. The proof is formal and is left to the reader.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6

Let \((X_i)\), \(i \in I\), be a generating family of \(\widetilde{C}\) (4.9). Then the family \(\mathrm{Lib}^\sim(X_i)\) is a generating family of \(\widetilde{C}_\gamma\).

Proof. The proof is formal once one has remarked that the functor \(\mathrm{esj}^\sim\) commutes with projective limits and that it is conservative (\(\mathrm{esj}^\sim(u)\) is an isomorphism \(\Longleftrightarrow\) \(u\) is an isomorphism).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.7

Let \(A\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf of rings, or else a small ring, \(\widetilde{C}_A\) (resp. \(\widehat{C}_A\)) the category of sheaves (resp. of presheaves) of unitary \(A\)-modules (6.3.3) on a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site \(C\). Then \(\widetilde{C}_A\) is an abelian \(\mathcal{U}\)-category satisfying the axioms (AB 5) ("existence of left exact filtered inductive limits") and (AB 3)* ("existence of infinite products") of [TOHOKU]. It possesses a family of generators indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Proof. It is clear that the category \(\widehat{C}_A\) is an abelian category satisfying the axioms (AB 3), (AB 4), and (AB 5) (I 2.8 and I 3.3). One then deduces from 6.4 that the category \(\widetilde{C}_A\) is an additive category in which the kernels and cokernels are representable. More precisely, let \(i_A\) and \(a_A\) be the inclusion functors into presheaves and associated sheaves and \(u : X \to Y\) a morphism of \(\widetilde{C}_A\). The functor \(a_A\) is left exact and commutes with inductive limits. The functor \(i_A\) commutes with projective limits. Consequently the functor \(i_A a_A : \widehat{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_A\) is a left exact additive functor. One deduces canonical isomorphisms: \[ (*) \qquad i_A(\mathrm{Ker}(u)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Ker}(i_A(u)) , \] \[ (**) \qquad \mathrm{coker}(u) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } a_A \mathrm{coker}(i_A(u)) . \] One consequently has a canonical isomorphism: \[ (***) \qquad \mathrm{coim}(u) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } a_A \mathrm{coim}(i_A(u)) . \] Let us show that the canonical morphism \(\mathrm{coim}(u) \to \mathrm{im}(u)\) is an isomorphism. For this, it suffices to show, by (*), that the sequence: \[ 0 \to i_A(\mathrm{coim}(u)) \to i_A(Y) \to i_A(\mathrm{coker}(u)) \] is exact. Using the isomorphisms (**) and (***) and remarking that \(a_A i_A(Y)\) is isomorphic to \(Y\), one sees that this sequence is isomorphic to the sequence: \[ 0 \to i_A a_A(\mathrm{coim}(i_A(u))) \to i_A a_A i_A(Y) \to i_A a_A(\mathrm{coker}(i_A(u))) , \] which is none other than the transform by the functor \(i_A a_A\) of the sequence: \[ 0 \to \mathrm{coim}(i_A(u)) \to i_A(Y) \to \mathrm{coker}(i_A(u)) . \] Now, this sequence is exact and the functor \(i_A a_A\) is left exact. The category \(\widetilde{C}_A\) is therefore an abelian category. The functor \(a_A : \widehat{C}_A \to \widetilde{C}_A\) is left exact and commutes with arbitrary inductive limits. Consequently it is additive, exact and commutes with inductive limits. The category \(\widehat{C}_A\) satisfying the axiom (AB 5), the same holds for the category \(\widetilde{C}_A\). Finally it is clear that in the category \(\widetilde{C}_A\), the products indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) are representable and, consequently, that the axiom (AB 3)* is satisfied, which completes the proof of the first assertion.

For every ring \(A\) an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), the functor: \[ \mathrm{esj} : \mathcal{U}\text{-}A\text{-module} \longrightarrow \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens} \] admits a left adjoint \(X_A\) (free \(A\)-module generated). It therefore suffices to apply 4.10 and 6.6 to complete the proof.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.html:
Notation 6.8

Let \(H\) be a sheaf of sets. The sheaf of \(A\)-modules associated to the presheaf (cf. notation 6.5) \[ X \mapsto \mathrm{Lib}_A H(X) \qquad X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C \] is denoted \(A_H\). When \(H = a(X)\) (sheaf associated to the presheaf represented by \(X\)) one writes sometimes simply \(A_X\) (by abuse of notation). The proof of 6.7 shows that the family of sheaves of \(A\)-modules \(A_X\), (\(X \in \mathrm{ob}(C)\)), is a generating family, indexed by an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), of the category of sheaves of \(A\)-modules.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.9

By [TOHOKU], 6.7 shows that the category \(\widetilde{C}_A\), when \(A\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), possesses enough injectives. One knows, moreover, that infinite products are not necessarily exact in \(\widetilde{C}_A\), and, consequently, that the category \(\widetilde{C}_A\) does not in general admit enough projectives [ROOS].
